findings.evidence: The mechanism and byte accounting appear in Chapter 7; Chapter 14 supplies the acceptance test.
findings.issue: Pointer form is inconsistent with the book's stated convention (Preface: 'Section cross-references use the § chapter.section form: a bare § N.M refers to chapter N, section M'). This paragraph uses bare 'Chapter N' prose pointers rather than § form, while adjacent paragraphs use '§5.3(a)' and '§5.7' forms (e.g. p. 111 'the §5.3(a)/§5.7 item still to validate'). The chapter-level pointer is acceptable but the surrounding text mixes three pointer styles in one section ('Chapter 3', 'Chapter 7', 'Chapter 14', '§5.3(a)', '§5.7'), and a reader following 'Chapter 14' cannot see which section of Ch. 14 carries the acceptance test.
findings.fix_instruction: Convert the pointer to a section-level pointer with the section title, e.g. '§14.2 (Acceptance test)', or state 'Chapter 14 §14.2 — Acceptance test' once and keep prose chapter pointers to chapter openers only.

findings.evidence: §2.3 shows that a single H100 cannot hold or stream the whole 140 GB model ... nor meet the prefill compute demand (1.19 PFLOPS required vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak, from 1.29 PFLOP / 1.08 s).
findings.issue: Pointer resolves to Ch. 2 §2.3 (Worked Example) correctly, but the quoted sentence omits the caveat that the cited page itself supplies in the same paragraph — 'This is a statement about the specified single-request, ~25 ms/token model, not about all possible 70B serving: batching, weight-read amortization, and precision changes (later chapters) fundamentally alter the per-request bandwidth demand' (p. 27). Repeating the 1.19-vs-0.989 verdict without the batching/amortization caveat makes the imported claim stronger than its source.
findings.fix_instruction: Extend the quoted claim with the source's own qualifier: '...nor meet the prefill compute demand (1.19 PFLOPS required vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak) under the batch-1-equivalent, no-amortization model of §2.3 — a device-feasibility illustration, not a capacity verdict for the canonical 8×H100 host'.

findings.evidence: 4.4.1. Model identity includes the execution path ... A loader may recognize the model while a fused attention operator, recurrent-state update or quantized expert kernel is unavailable on the target device.
findings.issue: This subsection is numbered 4.4.1 but sits inside Chapter 5 (From Workload to Model Selection). Chapter 5's own §5.4 is 'Measurement'; the subsection should be §5.4.1. The same defect appears in the book's own subsection-numbering convention elsewhere ('3.6.1. The 2026 baseline shift' inside Ch. 3 is correctly numbered, '7.3.1' inside Ch. 7 correctly). Any reader, indexer, or cross-referencing tool that resolves '§5.4.1' will fail to find it, and the section cannot be cited unambiguously because '§4.4.1' resolves to a different chapter's territory (Ch. 4 §4.4 is 'Measurement' and has no §4.4.1).
findings.fix_instruction: Renumber '4.4.1. Model identity includes the execution path' to '5.4.1', and add a rule to the house style that a subsection's number is always <chapter>.<section>.<subsection>.

findings.evidence: Chapter 5's 9,000 tokens per dollar is single-stream (50 tok/s), while this chapter's ~2.76M input tokens per $1 of fleet spend (~2.85M combined) is whole-fleet aggregate.
findings.issue: Reconciliation note compares '2.85M combined tokens per $1' against Ch. 5's '~285,000 tokens per dollar' — a 10× ratio that is never numerically reconciled, only labeled as 'whole-fleet aggregate' vs 'single-stream'. Check: Ch. 5's 285,000 tokens/$ derives from 1,583 tok/s ÷ $20/hr. Ch. 4's 2.85M combined tokens/$ derives from (92,000 + 3,000) tok/s ÷ $120/hr = 95000/120 = 791.7 tok/s per $ → × 3,600 = 2.85M per $. The two quantities have different numerators and different denominators (one host's price vs the whole fleet's price), so a reader cannot see why the whole-fleet figure is 10× the single-host figure. The note's parenthetical labels the difference of kind but supplies no bridge, and the two figures will be quoted side by side in a procurement discussion.
findings.fix_instruction: Extend the reconciliation note with the numeric bridge: 'Ch. 4's figure divides the whole fleet's offered rate (95,000 tok/s) by the whole fleet's spend ($120/hr → 6 hosts); Ch. 5's divides one host's single-stream rate (1,583 tok/s) by one host's price ($20/hr). The 10× gap is the fleet's aggregate rate, not a contradiction; do not mix a whole-fleet numerator with a per-host denominator.'

findings.evidence: FLOPs per embedding = 2 × params × L at a 64-token query (L = 64); the value scales linearly with query length, so the model-to-model ratio equals the parameter ratio (bge-large ≈ 3× mpnet). Note: 2 × params × L treats the token-embedding table as a per-position matmul; it is a lookup, so the proxy overstates compute — most for the smallest model (MiniLM's table is ~51% of its params).
findings.issue: The table's GFLOP values are computed with the stated proxy (2 × params × 64): all-MiniLM-L6-v2 ~23M × 2 × 64 = 2.94 GFLOP ✓ (printed ~2.9); all-mpnet-base-v2 ~110M × 2 × 64 = 14.08 GFLOP ✓ (printed ~14); bge-large-en ~335M × 2 × 64 = 42.9 GFLOP ✓ (printed ~43). The ratio claim 'bge-large ≈ 3× mpnet' is 42.88/14.08 = 3.05 ✓. But the table header says 'Params' with values ~23M / ~110M / ~335M and the note says 'the model-to-model ratio equals the parameter ratio' — the parameter ratio mpnet/MiniLM is 110/23 = 4.78 and the GFLOP ratio is 14.08/2.94 = 4.79 ✓, but the prose in §5.3(a) then says 'body-parameter ratios are the truer cross-model comparison (mpnet/MiniLM ~7.7× body-only vs 4.8× by total params)'. The 7.7× figure is introduced with no derivation in the table or the note; the reader cannot reproduce it from the printed parameter counts (which are totals, not body-only).
findings.fix_instruction: Show the body-only derivation for the ~7.7× figure (e.g. the parameter counts excluding the embedding table, with the table sizes stated) so the number is reproducible, and add the body-only parameter column to Table 5-1 rather than citing the ratio in prose only.

findings.evidence: ~186–371 ms if encoded on a single CPU core at ~30–60 GFLOP/s sustained ... but only ~1.1 ms on a ~10 TFLOP/s GPU ... single-core encoding fits only above ≈92.8 GFLOP/s sustained per core (11.14 GFLOP ÷ 0.12 s), beyond the typical sustained range (371 ms at 30 GFLOP/s vs 186 ms at 60 GFLOP/s)
findings.issue: Recomputation: 11.14 ÷ 30 = 0.371 s ✓; 11.14 ÷ 60 = 0.186 s ✓; 11.14 ÷ 0.12 = 92.8 GFLOP/s ✓; 11.14 GFLOP ÷ 10 TFLOP/s = 1.114 ms ✓. The arithmetic is sound. The defect is a unit-basis inconsistency inside the same paragraph: the CPU figures use the *incremental* cost of mpnet over MiniLM (11.14 GFLOP), while the GPU figure of 1.1 ms also uses the incremental 11.14 GFLOP — but the §5.3(a) table's own rows are absolute per-embedding costs (2.94 GFLOP for MiniLM, 14.08 for mpnet), and the §5.3(a) bullet describes the comparison as 'the incremental per-request compute cost of the 768-dim (all-mpnet) vs 384-dim (MiniLM) embedding models — a cross-model difference, not a dim-only sweep'. A reader comparing the ~1.1 ms GPU figure against the ~120 ms retrieval budget will read it as the embedding cost, when it is the *difference* between two models. The §5.3(a) hypothesis bullet also says 'a 384-dim variant of the same model family can halve the index storage ... (the encoder's compute is essentially unchanged)', which contradicts the framing of the 11.14 GFLOP as an intra-family dim-sweep delta.
findings.fix_instruction: State explicitly in the sentence: 'this is the mpnet-minus-MiniLM delta, not either model's absolute per-embedding cost (2.94 GFLOP for MiniLM, 14.08 GFLOP for mpnet at a 64-token query)'. Separate the two claims: the cross-model delta (11.14 GFLOP) and the within-family dim-sweep delta (~0 GFLOP encoder, storage halved) — they are different experiments and should not share a bullet.

findings.evidence: Total tokens per dollar (serial single-stream floor, no overlap; 20 ms/token basis) ~242,000 tokens per dollar (~199,000 at the canonical 25 ms/token) 9,500/7.08 ≈ 1,342 tok/s × 3600 ÷ $20; 7.08 s = 1.08 s prefill + 6.0 s decode at the illustrative 20 ms/token rate
findings.issue: Recomputation: 9,500/7.08 = 1,342 tok/s ✓; 1,342 × 3,600 ÷ 20 = 241,560 ≈ 242,000 ✓; 9,500/8.58 = 1,107 tok/s ✓; 1,107 × 3,600 ÷ 20 = 199,260 ≈ 199,000 ✓. The arithmetic is sound. The consistency defect is that this row's 'total tokens per dollar' includes both input and output tokens (9,500/request), while the row above it — 'Output tokens per dollar (single-stream decode, 50 tok/s): 9,000 output tokens per dollar' — is output-only, and the row above that — '~285,000 tokens per dollar' — is a combined-token figure computed as 50 × (1 + 9,200/300) = 1,583 tok/s. Three different token-bases appear in one table with 'tokens per dollar' in each row label: output-only (9,000), combined-with-overlap (285,000), combined-serial (242,000/199,000). The row labels do specify the basis, but the Ch. 4 reconciliation note compares only two of them (9,000 and 285,000), leaving the 242,000/199,000 pair unreconciled with either.
findings.fix_instruction: Extend the reconciliation note to cover all four rows in one table: output-only 9,000; combined overlapped 285,000; combined serial at 20 ms/token 242,000; combined serial at 25 ms/token 199,000 — with a single statement that all four are single-stream floors of the same host and that the host's aggregate batched counterpart is Ch. 15's ~35,000–56,000 tok/s.

findings.evidence: 5.5. Common Mistakes • Starting with 'which model is best?' Instead of characterizing the workload first.
findings.issue: The bullet opens with a fragment ('Instead of characterizing the workload first.') rather than a full sentence naming the mistake, unlike every other bullet in the book's Common Mistakes lists (which use 'Treating X as Y.', 'Using X at Y.', 'Quoting X as free capacity.'). The fragment's referent ('the workload first') is only recoverable from the bullet title, and the bullet then continues with a second, separate claim ('a model short-circuits the reasoning chain and leads to post hoc justification') that could stand as its own bullet.
findings.fix_instruction: Rewrite as a complete bullet in the house form: 'Starting with 'which model is best?' instead of characterizing the workload. Model selection is a consequence of workload characterization; starting with a model short-circuits the reasoning chain and produces post hoc justification.'

findings.evidence: [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] — not a reference measurement): for the canonical workload, a well-designed RAG + guardrails pipeline may approach a fine-tuned model's answer quality on in-domain queries.
findings.issue: A stray closing parenthesis and an unbalanced bracket: the sentence opens with '([ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] — not a reference measurement):' and then the paragraph carries no closing marker before the next sentence, so the parenthetical swallows the following sentence 'This is task-, model-, data-, and evaluation-dependent'. The tag pair is also applied to a hedged quality claim rather than to a number — the book's declared Axis 1/2 pair system (Preface p. 17) governs quantitative claims, and this sentence contains none, so the tag reads as a provenance mark on a qualitative assertion.
findings.fix_instruction: Close the parenthetical correctly and keep the tag adjacent to the claim it qualifies: 'a well-designed RAG + guardrails pipeline may approach a fine-tuned model's answer quality on in-domain queries [HYPOTHESIS] — not a reference measurement; task-, model-, data- and evaluation-dependent.' Use [HYPOTHESIS] (the book's tag for reasoned-but-unvalidated claims) rather than [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] for a non-quantitative assertion.

findings.evidence: PDF p. 110 (Printed Page 90): "[1P][DERIVED] [HYPOTHESIS] : within a given embedding family..." PDF p. 112 (Printed Page 92): "[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]: for a 1 M‑chunk corpus..."
findings.issue: Evidence label syntax violation and logical mismatch. On page 110, a double label `[1P][DERIVED] [HYPOTHESIS]` is used, violating the Preface's definition that a label pair consists of exactly one item from Axis 1 and one from Axis 2. Furthermore, on page 112, the corpus size of 1M chunks is used to derive index storage but is labeled `[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]` even though the exact same corpus size was defined earlier as a fixed `[HYPOTHESIS]` input on page 110.
findings.fix_instruction: Fix the label syntax on p. 110 by removing the redundant `[1P][DERIVED]` pair and leaving only `[HYPOTHESIS]`. Ensure consistent provenance tagging across p. 110–112 by defining the 1M-chunk size explicitly once as a `[canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]` or `[ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]`.

findings.evidence: PDF p. 109, Figure 3.2 (PDF p. 59): "Convention: the source box’s fixed tokens are drawn outside the canvas; cells show output positions only, and accepted IDs extend the prefix." PDF p. 60 (Printed Page 40), Table 3-2: "Active parameters per token (top-2 routing) ~12.8B"
findings.issue: Missing semantic link between Figure 3.2 and MoE text. The text in Chapter 3 heavily uses the active parameter count (~12.8B) to justify memory savings on HBM reads. However, Figure 3.2 discusses 'accepted IDs' and dependency orders but doesn't specify if the 'active weights' are read *once* per token or *once per accepted sequence*. In autoregressive decoding, the weight reads happen once per forward pass (1 token). The book is technically correct elsewhere, but Figure 3.2 doesn't explicitly link the token position in the autoregressive flow to the parameter activation shown in Figure 3.4's MoE panel, making the visual bridge from mechanism (Fig 3.2) to math (Fig 3.4) a bit disjointed.
findings.fix_instruction: Consider adding an explicit arrow or caption in Figure 3.2 panel A linking the single token forward pass to the active parameters calculation in Figure 3.4.
